vignette:
# Kofi

Kofi was thirty-two when the war came to his neighborhood in Freetown. He had been a teacher then, unmarried, living with his mother in a modest house three streets back from the main road. On the morning of January 6th, 1999, he woke to the sound of automatic weapons and the smell of smoke. The rebels had breached the city's eastern perimeter during the night. By afternoon, soldiers were moving through the residential quarters, and Kofi, along with a dozen neighbors sheltering in a nearby compound, made the choice to run toward the university grounds, where they believed peacekeepers were stationed. They never made it. Two blocks from safety, a building ahead of them caught fire—a petrol station, or perhaps a house where fuel had been stored—and the flames spread with terrifying speed across the street, cutting off their route. Kofi and four others doubled back into the maze of side streets, separated from the rest. In the chaos, a young boy, no more than ten, who had been running alongside them, was shot. Kofi carried him for two blocks before the child died in his arms. He made it to the university alone. Forty-three people from his neighborhood did not.

For fifteen years after the war ended, Kofi built a life of deliberate normalcy. He emigrated to the United States at thirty-five, retrained as a park ranger, and took a position managing a large state forest in the Pacific Northwest. The work suited him—solitude, structure, the illusion of control. But in the past three years, the symptoms had become impossible to ignore. Any criticism from his supervisor, even the gentlest correction about a maintenance report or a protocol deviation, sent him into a spiral of shame and anger. He had come to believe that he was fundamentally corrupt, that his survival while others perished was a mark of cowardice or complicity he could never wash away. Once he had settled into this conviction—that he was marked, irredeemably flawed—the world seemed to reorganize itself around confirmation of it. His belief that he was fundamentally corrupted meant that almost anything could become a trigger, a piece of evidence that danger was closing in: a supervisor's gentle suggestion about fieldwork became an accusation; the smell of smoke on the wind became a test of his worthiness; even the sight of a uniform in his apartment complex felt like an indictment waiting to happen. Once he had settled into this conviction—that he was marked, irredeemably flawed—the world seemed to reorganize itself around confirmation of it. A supervisor's gentle suggestion about fieldwork became an accusation; the smell of smoke on the wind became a test of his worthiness; even the sight of a uniform in his apartment complex felt like an indictment waiting to happen. When his supervisor had suggested last spring that Kofi needed to spend more time in the field doing prescribed burns—a routine part of forest management—Kofi had felt the criticism as an accusation, and within weeks, he had begun to isolate. He stopped answering calls from the two colleagues who had tried to befriend him. He avoided the ranger station entirely, claiming illness, until his supervisor grew concerned enough to mandate a fitness-for-duty evaluation.

The prescribed burns were the real turning point. Fire had become a trigger—not just the memory of that January morning, but the very sight of flames in any form. When Kofi was required to oversee a controlled burn in a section of old-growth forest, the smell of smoke and the crackling advance of the fire line sent him into a state of hypervigilance that lasted for days. He couldn't sleep that night or the next. His mind raced with catastrophic interpretations: the fire would escape containment, people would die because of his incompetence, he would be responsible for another tragedy. He was certain that any delay in the burn crew's response to a flare-up meant disaster was unfolding, that something terrible was about to happen. The inability to relax, even sitting in his apartment afterward with all doors locked and the windows closed, was suffocating. He found himself reaching for alcohol more frequently—a beer or two in the evening became a nightly ritual, then two became four. He also began to avoid anything that resembled authority or enforcement: he stopped watching news broadcasts, avoided police checkpoints, and refused to attend a community safety meeting at his apartment complex because he couldn't bear the sight of the uniformed officers stationed outside.

The isolation deepened his conviction that he was fundamentally damaged and unfit for human connection. In the quiet of his apartment, alone with his thoughts, the guilt consumed him—why had that boy died and not him? What had he done, or failed to do, that made him worthy of survival? The drinking and the avoidance had kept him safe, in his nervous system's accounting—they had prevented him from being exposed, from facing the judgment he deserved—which meant the threat they were responding to must be real and ongoing. Without ever testing the feeling, without ever staying in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, his body had never received the evidence it needed to believe otherwise; the danger remained as high as the day he carried that boy's body through the streets. The more deeply he believed himself fundamentally corrupted by survival, the more his mind treated ordinary sensations—a crackling sound at night, the acrid smell of distant smoke, the sight of emergency vehicles—as harbingers of the reckoning he deserved. His conviction that he was unfit for normal life meant that almost anything could become a trigger, a piece of evidence that danger was closing in. The more he drank, the more he withdrew, the more his sense of isolation crystallized into a felt certainty that he was marked, separated from normal life by something irreversible. The drinking and the avoidance had kept him safe, in his nervous system's accounting—they had prevented him from being exposed, from facing the judgment he deserved—which meant the threat they were responding to must be real and ongoing. Without ever testing the feeling, without ever staying in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, his body had never received the evidence it needed to believe otherwise; the danger remained as high as the day he carried that boy's body through the streets. Being in nature, which had once been his refuge, had become another minefield. A hike through the forest—something he used to do for solace—now triggered the same hypervigilance, the same sense that he was back in those streets, that danger was imminent. Even the sight of a distant brush fire on the news would send him into a state of dread that lingered for hours. The drinking helped briefly, dulling the edge, but it also meant he was no longer sleeping, and the exhaustion fed back into his threat sensitivity—every unexpected sound at night felt like a warning, every delay in a phone call from his mother felt like proof that something catastrophic was happening.

Three weeks ago, his supervisor informed him that if he did not complete a mental health evaluation and begin treatment, his position would be terminated. Kofi finally called a therapist. He sits now in the waiting room, hands trembling slightly, uncertain whether he can trust anyone with the truth of what he carries—the guilt, the shame, the conviction that he is fundamentally broken and that the world is far more dangerous than anyone else seems to understand.

The drinking and the avoidance had kept him safe, in his nervous system's accounting—they had prevented him from being exposed, from facing the judgment he deserved—which meant the threat they were responding to must be real and ongoing. Without ever testing the feeling, without ever staying in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, his body had never received the evidence it needed to believe otherwise; the danger remained as high as the day he carried that boy's body through the streets. Being in nature, which had once been his refuge, had become another minefield. A hike through the forest—something he used to do for solace—now triggered the same hypervigilance, the same sense that he was back in those streets, that danger was imminent. Even the sight of a distant brush fire on the news would send him into a state of dread that lingered for hours. The drinking helped briefly, dulling the edge, but it also meant he was no longer sleeping, and the exhaustion fed back into his threat sensitivity—every unexpected sound at night felt like a warning, every delay in a phone call from his mother felt like proof that something catastrophic was happening.

Three weeks ago, his supervisor informed him that if he did not complete a mental health evaluation and begin treatment, his position would be terminated. Kofi finally called a therapist. He sits now in the waiting room, hands trembling slightly, uncertain whether he can trust anyone with the truth of what he carries—the guilt, the shame, the conviction that he is fundamentally broken and that the world is far more dangerous than anyone else seems to understand.
